pages.text: On the way to school, Ofei and Gbeddy saw smoke. A heap of rubbish was burning by the road. The smoke stung their eyes. “Cough, cough,” coughed Ofei. “My chest hurts.”
sentences: On the way to school, Ofei and Gbeddy saw smoke.
A heap of rubbish was burning by the road.
The smoke stung their eyes.
“Cough, cough,” coughed Ofei.
“My chest hurts.”
pages.alt: Walking along a red-earth town path toward school, Ofei and Gbeddy step back and cover their noses as grey smoke drifts from a smouldering roadside rubbish heap in the distance.

pages.text: At school, they told their teacher. “Smoke from burning rubbish makes the air dirty,” she said. “It can make people cough, and hurt eyes and chests. Plastic smoke is the worst.”
sentences: At school, they told their teacher.
“Smoke from burning rubbish makes the air dirty,” she said.
“It can make people cough, and hurt eyes and chests.
Plastic smoke is the worst.”
pages.alt: Inside a bright Ghanaian classroom, Ofei and Gbeddy speak earnestly to their attentive teacher in a green patterned dress.

pages.text: “So what should we do with rubbish?” asked Gbeddy. “We can reuse some things and put the rest in a bin,” said the teacher. “Food waste can go into a compost heap. Never burn plastic.”
sentences: “So what should we do with rubbish?” asked Gbeddy.
“We can reuse some things and put the rest in a bin,” said the teacher.
“Food waste can go into a compost heap.
Never burn plastic.”
pages.alt: Outside by the school garden, the teacher points toward a tidy covered waste bin and a wooden-slatted garden compost heap.

pages.text: The class set up three colour-coded boxes: one for reuse, one for compost and one for the bin. Ofei put a clean bottle in the reuse box. Gbeddy put banana skins in the compost box. They agreed that children never light fires, and always tell a grown-up.
sentences: The class set up three colour-coded boxes: one for reuse, one for compost and one for the bin.
Ofei put a clean bottle in the reuse box.
Gbeddy put banana skins in the compost box.
They agreed that children never light fires, and always tell a grown-up.
pages.alt: In the classroom, Ofei places a clean plastic bottle into an unlabelled blue box while Gbeddy drops banana peels into an unlabelled green box beside a yellow bin.

pages.text: The class took a polite letter in a sealed envelope to the elders. “Please help us find a safe place for rubbish, and a way to collect it,” they asked. The elders listened and spoke to the town’s waste collectors.
sentences: The class took a polite letter in a sealed envelope to the elders.
“Please help us find a safe place for rubbish, and a way to collect it,” they asked.
The elders listened and spoke to the town’s waste collectors.
pages.alt: Under a shady compound tree alongside their teacher, Ofei and Gbeddy respectfully hand a plain white envelope to a smiling elder wrapped in traditional cloth.

pages.text: A few weeks later, the heap by the road was gone. The air was clean. “We can breathe!” said Ofei. “Clean air is for everybody,” said Gbeddy. “We must look after it.”

pages.alt: Under a clear blue morning sky beside a clean grassy roadside with fresh green trees, Ofei and Gbeddy walk happily to school breathing fresh air.
